name: Carlos Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, with a vocational certificate and apprenticeship behind me, and I repair overhead power lines for an electricity company near the coast. On a dry day we change poles and worn fittings; after a storm we rebuild whatever the wind has dropped. I like restoring a whole street, but long wet shifts take more out of me now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works as a nurse, and our children are grown and independent. My lineworker pay is above the usual rate, we have about ten months of expenses saved and several other utilities nearby, so retirement is in sight but we have not fixed the date. I use AI every day to sort storm photographs and check weather windows, then I have the crew verify the actual line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the storm crew AI is a useful helper, not a replacement for people hauling wire through wet sand. I use it daily to sort damage photos, but a worker still tests and rebuilds a downed line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair shifts and my partner's nursing work look steady. With ten months of expenses saved, good pay and other utility crews nearby, I can keep discussing retirement without a deadline forced by technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on the coastal storm rota and use my current AI photo sorter for the next callout. Before assigning a truck, I'll compare each flagged pole with the crew's site report and the feeder map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little disappointed that the tools stop at convenience. The next storm still gives me enough real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where has the photo sorter sent you wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month we checked a suspicious pole photograph against the feeder map. The AI photo sorter marked sea spray as a broken insulator; our crew found the cracked crossarm two streets away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change a household plan in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would leave the family holiday as planned. We are not spending from the emergency account on a new AI device just because a vendor calls it clever.

say: **AI photos** can help sort damage, while crews still test and rebuild storm-damaged lines.
**Site reports** and feeder maps should settle where the truck goes.
think: My **storm shifts** and my partner's nursing work look secure.
Our **ten-month reserve** and nearby utilities leave room to plan retirement carefully.
do: **Keep** the coastal storm repair rota and current AI photo sorter.
**Compare** flagged poles with crew reports and feeder maps before dispatch.
feel: **Calm** about wages, mildly disappointed by limited technology change.
S0.quote: The AI photo sorter marked sea spray as a broken insulator; our crew found the cracked crossarm two streets away.
fieldNote: He already uses **AI daily**, while a wrong spray label shows why crew checks remain.
Strong savings, partner nursing income and **nearby jobs** make the plateau financially easy.

steps.text: Keep coastal storm repair rota and current photo sorter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may book trucks and buy parts before robots can rebuild lines after a storm. Give a crew the revised map, then let it say which road is under water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical repair hours still look strong, especially on storm nights. The problem is a dispatcher cut leaving us with too many unchecked routes, and I do not want a younger crew sent into the dark on a bad map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll put the approved AI route planner beside three recent storm maps and mark the blocked roads it misses. If it passes a field check, I'll learn its editing controls on paid time and show a younger crew how to report a wrong route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about safety and who checks the map; I don't expect my own pay to fall soon. I can work with a proven tool and still insist on a human correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the route crosses floodwater?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the truck at the dry junction and call control with the road closure. A screen can draw a route through floodwater; our power-line truck cannot drive it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else needs the corrected road closure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the dispatcher to mark that closure on every crew map, not only ours. If nobody is left in dispatch to do it, the company must assign a named person before the next storm.

say: **AI routes** can help dispatch, but field crews must correct flooded roads.
**Named dispatch checks** matter when office posts shrink before field robots spread.
think: My **storm repair hours** look likely to hold in this slower change.
Fewer **dispatchers** could make night work riskier for younger crews.
do: **Test** approved AI routes against three recent storm maps.
**Learn** planner editing controls on paid time if field checks pass.
feel: **Uneasy** about safety handoffs, while expecting stable repair income.
S1.quote: A screen can draw a route through floodwater; our power-line truck cannot drive it.
fieldNote: He wants to test **three past storms** before adopting new route controls.
His concern is **shared safety information** during storms, not a claimed personal wage loss.

steps.text: Test approved AI routes against three storm maps
Learn planner editing controls on paid time if field checks pass

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 will change dispatch first, while capable field robots around 2031 might rebuild ordinary spans. Storm damage is messy, but I will not bet my storm-line wages on repair robots failing forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be about 63 when those robots reach line repair. We have ten months saved and my partner's nursing pay, yet a large cut in my storm hours before retirement is affordable would still change our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the company for its 2028 dispatch and 2031 field crew numbers. I'll put my name forward for a paid robot repair pilot with real controls if offered, and my partner and I will review retirement income before changing our work plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a realistic loss of paid storm shifts, though I have skills and local employers to approach. I would rather test the machines than guess at the staffing number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown son that we have a buffer and are asking about work, not asking him to help with our bills. He is building his own household now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a paid robot pilot worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect normal pay and a real stop control in any pilot. A demonstration watched from behind a barrier would teach me nothing about taking responsibility on a broken line.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch before field robots reach repairs around 2031.
The company should publish **crew numbers** rather than promise storm work will never change.
think: At about **63**, a large cut in storm hours could arrive before retirement is affordable.
Our **ten-month reserve** and partner wage buy time, not a guarantee of unchanged income.
do: **Ask** company for 2028 dispatch and 2031 field crew numbers.
**Join** paid robot repair pilot if offered with normal pay and stop controls.
**Review** retirement income with partner before changing work plans.
feel: **Anxious** about possible storm-hour loss, with financial and job options.
S2.quote: I will not bet my storm-line wages on repair robots failing forever.
fieldNote: He recognises **field robots** as a later wage risk despite his hands-on storm skill.
His paid pilot includes **control use**, not passive watching.
Retirement review stays an **enquiry**, with no early retirement decision.

steps.text: Ask company for dispatch and field crew numbers
Join paid repair pilot if normal pay and stop controls offered
Review retirement income with partner before changing work plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes planning first, and capable repair robots around 2034 arrive when I will be about 66. Five years gives me a chance to see whether I can choose retirement before robot crews reshape the field roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might want a paid storm-training role at 66 if the budget says I need more wages. The company has not offered one. A few storm-training talks cannot replace the power-line shifts that pay my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep a record of our storm repair methods for the company training yard, and ask what full-wage trainer vacancies actually exist. My partner and I will review retirement income yearly, and I'll apply only if a trainer job is posted with pay that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about whether a paid role will be there if I still need it. I have years to find out, but I want the answer in wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach from your storm notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a new worker how to set a temporary support before replacing a snapped pole. My field notes would be a starting point; the trainee must practise with a real crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a training role a real job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full-wage training vacancy needs paid hours on a practice line and a roster I can rely on. If those pieces are missing, I will keep repairing storms while my body allows.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes planning before 2034 field robots affect repairs.
A **full-wage trainer role** matters only if storm crews actually need fewer workers.
think: At about **66**, I may still need wages if retirement calculations fall short.
No **trainer vacancy** has been offered, so occasional talks cannot replace shifts.
do: **Record** storm repair methods for the company training yard.
**Check** full-wage storm trainer vacancies and required field hours.
**Review** retirement income with partner each year before applying.
feel: **Uneasy** about later paid work if retirement is not affordable.
S3.quote: A few storm-training talks cannot replace the power-line shifts that pay my bills.
fieldNote: The 2034 robot date falls near **age 66**, when retirement may or may not work.
His training idea is **conditional paid employment**, not an existing second income.

steps.text: Record storm repair methods for company training yard
Check full-wage storm trainer vacancies and field hours
Review retirement income with partner annually before applying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 and field robots around 2039 arrive after the age I hope to stop storm callouts. The younger crews should still practise rebuilding a line with their own hands before trusting a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 71 when field robots arrive, and I expect to be off the storm rota if our retirement budget holds. The longer timetable leaves my own wages less exposed, but it does not settle a date by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I will review our savings and expected retirement income, then set a yearly check of household spending. I'll keep taking storm shifts while it is safe, and hand my repair notes to a younger crew member before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this technology timetable. I would like to stop working because our finances allow it, not because a machine has driven us out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown daughter about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown daughter to choose her own trade, but to ask how much real practice its apprentices get. A storm crew that has only watched repair robots will struggle when floodwater closes the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hand a younger storm worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The handover would include the maps of blocked roads and the order we rebuild feeders after a flood. I would sit with a younger worker at the depot and explain why the order matters.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes planning before field robots reach storm repair around 2039.
**Apprentice practice** should include rebuilding lines by hand before relying on robots.
think: At about **71**, I expect to be off storm callouts if retirement figures work.
My **exit date** remains conditional on household income and safe working capacity.
do: **Review** savings and expected retirement income with partner this year.
**Keep** storm shifts while safe and affordable to continue.
**Hand** blocked-road maps and repair notes to younger lineworker before leaving.
feel: **Calm** about the long runway, wanting a careful handover.
S4.quote: A storm crew that has only watched repair robots will struggle when floodwater closes the road.
fieldNote: He expects **less personal exposure** to 2039 robots, subject to retirement finances.
The handover includes **specific maps** and repair order, fitting his own storm work.

steps.text: Review retirement savings and income with partner this year
Keep storm shifts while safe and affordable to continue

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots arrive around 2031, when I will be about 63 and may still need my storm wages. A written crew plan, a paid control trial and real retirement income figures would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the next crew to rebuild a feeder when a storm closes every road. My phone can sort storm photographs, but a younger lineworker needs the map and a person who has carried wire through floodwater. I want time to make that handover properly.

headlineQuote: My phone can sort storm photographs, but a younger lineworker needs the map and a person who has carried wire through floodwater.
portrait: **Carlos**, 58, repairs coastal overhead lines after a vocational apprenticeship and works long storm restoration shifts.
He uses **AI daily** for damage photographs but checks its guesses against feeder maps and site reports.
His **higher pay**, nursing partner, ten-month savings and nearby utilities give room to plan retirement.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about lost storm wages at 63; later dates turn his focus toward paid training roles and handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring repair robots around 2031 while he still needs storm wages.
whatWouldHelp: A written **crew plan**, paid control trial and real retirement-income figures would help him choose.
